newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: OPINION - Crisis in SAfrica gold mines - By E.Osborn.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - Crisis in SAfrica gold mines - By E.Osborn.

text.p: By Edward Osborn, consultant to Edey, Rogers (Pty) Ltd

The story of the South African economy over the last 25 years has been one of an enormous structural change represented by an ageing gold mining industry in conjunction with the growth of the rest of the economy.

Although its contribution to the gross domestic product of the country has been receding, activity in the gold mining industry grew right through to the end of the 1980s, reaching its peak in 1989. Since then both contribution to GDP and level of activity has slipped back.

In 1970 the gold mining industry contributed almost 20 percent to GDP, but by 1980 the contribution had fallen to nine percent and by 1990 to seven percent. In terms of value added at constant prices, gold mining declined by a third between 1970 and 1980 and by a further seven percent during the 1980s. Clearly there was a distinct slowdown in the rate of decline in the importance of the industry.

But, on the other hand, the activity involved in wresting gold from the ground, in terms of manpower, electricity and stores consumed and the like, as encapsulated in the tonnage of ore milled, rose from 74.4 million tonnes in 1970 to 89.9 million tonnes in 1980 and reached a peak of 113.7 million tonnes in 1989. Since then it has fallen back to 91.7 million tonnes in 1996.

In essence, the industry has grown in size over the years but has declined in substance. The key to this apparent contradiction is, of course, the average grade of ore mined. As deeper level mining has occurred the grades have deteriorated and greater mining effort has been required. Thus the average grade for the industry was 13.3 grams per ton in 1970, down to 7.3 grams in 1980, and 5.1 grams in 1990. It has stabilised at about the five gram level during the 1990s.

Incidentally, while the gold mining industry was receding the rest of the economy was growing, initially at a strong average pace of 4.5 percent per annum in the 1970s. The average growth rate in the 1980s was very much more pedestrian at 1.7 percent per annum, partly because the economy had reached a degree of maturity, but primarily due to the constraining sanctions measures taken against South Africa. Gold mining was broadly unaffected by these measures but had its own intrinsic problems of declining grade and rapidly rising cost inflation.

On the basis of working costs per tonne of ore milled, inflation from one year to the next averaged 15.8 percent during the 1980s. Related to a kg of gold produced the average working cost inflation was as much as 21.7 percent per annum.

The industry would not have been able to survive at all if it had not been for the decline in the rand as the international gold price was certainly not accommodating, falling back from the spike of $613 per ounce averaged in 1980 to a depressed $141 in 1985, but recovering to $381 in 1989. The effective rand price rose from 477 rand in 1980 to 400 in 1991 to almost 1,000 in 1989.

But by 1990 the industry was in real crisis because of the persistent high internal inflation of working costs. This had to be brought to a halt and radical technological changes were introduced in the industry, which, unfortunately, were at the expense of manpower employed. The industry dropped employment by nearly 100,000 during 1990 and 1991 and this induced the recession in the country that lasted until 1993. Per kg working cost inflation dropped sharply to 9.9 percent in 1990 and was almost eliminated altogether in 1992. However, working cost inflation has since risen sharply, reaching an unacceptable peak of 19.5 percent in 1995, followed by a further 10.8 percent rise in 1996.

Boosted by the massive devaluation of the rand in the mid-eighties the working profit of the mines that are the members of the Chamber of Mines and which comprise the major part of the industry has fallen back to much lower levels of profitability depending on the relative movements of cost inflation and average rand realisations.

The lowest level of profitability in the last fifteen years occurred in 1995 when profits won amount to 3.4 billion rand as a result of the virtually stable rand in the face of a 19.5 percent rise in working costs per kg. A renewed crisis faced the industry. In the final quarter of 1995, for example, nearly half of the mines, representing 30 percent of total national production, were producing at a loss excluding capex. With capex brought to account in the costs of operation, two-thirds of the mines, representing half of national production, were functioning at a loss.

The industry was salvaged during 1996 because of the sharp correction of a patently overvalued rand. For the year as a whole the rand average gold price rose 19.5 percent to 1,664 rand an ounce, as opposed to a 10.8 percent rise in working costs per kg. The industry was further assisted by an average four percent rise in grades in the year.

The best quarter was the most recent final quarter of 1996 when working profits amounted to 1,520 million rand, as compared with 817 million the year before. The average grade was relatively high at 5.4 grams per ton and a record working revenue of 1,741 rand per ounce was realised in the quarter. The year-on-year inflation of working costs per ounce was a moderate 11 percent but a fearsome 23 percent per tonne milled.

In this final quarter the entire industry operated at a profit, albeit with a very wide distribution of profitability from 753 rand to two rand an ounce. That is without capex taken into account. But with capex brought into the picture nearly half of the number of reporting mines, but representing 24.5 percent of national production, operated at a loss.

A sharp reversal of the fortunes of the industry is now in prospect because of the recent strengthening of the rand for much the same cause of rand strength in 1995, namely foreign portfolio investment. The unfortunate coincident weakening of the international gold price will be a contributing factor. On the assumptions of an average grade of five grams per tonne, an inflation of working costs per tonne from quarter-to-quarter of five percent, and an average working revenue falling back to 1,615 rand per ounce, working profit will collapse in the first quarter of 1997 to a mere 270 million rand -- as compared with the 1,520 million rand in the fourth quarter of 1996.

Because of the wide distribution of working costs half of national production will be at a loss without capex considerations and with the same relative levels of capex maintained nearly the entire industry will operate at a loss.

The foreign investor and foreign central bank sales of gold will be the death of us unless there is a quantum leap in productivity in the industry. A reduced number of public holidays, the introduction of full calendar operations and the introduction of flexible working practices make this possible.
(The opinions expressed in this article represent those of the author only. They should not be seen to represent the views of Reuters.)
